subject: botany
question_text: What are the different branches of Botany that deal with the morphology of plants? Give their salient features.

verification.note: Sourced from the Telangana Junior Fastrack botany guide, Chapter 3 'Science of Plants' (book pp.5-6). The botany book prints NO star ranks and NO year citations, so stars=0 and appearances=[] record absence of signal, not measured frequency. Only ONE botany source is held — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand is physics-only and no botany board paper exists in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the board-paper back-test are both structurally impossible for botany: 'unverified' means never yet checkable against a second source, not checked-and-clean. The 1+1+1+1 split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The card keeps the syllabus framing the book prints — histology (tissues) and anatomy (gross internal details) as the two branches of internal morphology — which is the framing that is marked.

steps.label: Morphology defined
lines: Morphology deals with the study and
description of the different organs of a
plant. It is a fundamental requirement for
the classification of plants. It has two
steps.why: The answer opens with what morphology is and why it matters: organs are described first, and classification is built on those descriptions.
common_mistakes: Defining physiology (functions) instead of morphology (form and organs).
Dropping the classification line — 'fundamental for classification' is a marked feature.
steps.memory_tip: Morphology = form. Describe the organs first; classification follows from the description.
steps.margin_note: Definition plus the classification line, then announce the two parts.

steps.label: External morphology
lines: a) External morphology is the study and
description of the external characters of
plant organs such as root, stem, leaf,
steps.why: The first branch covers what is visible from outside; the six organs, root to seed, are the standard list to name.
common_mistakes: Naming fewer organs — root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit and seed is the expected list.
Writing 'outside of the cell' — external here means the outside of the plant's organs, not of cells.
steps.memory_tip: Six organs from bottom to top: root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit, seed.
steps.margin_note: One sentence with the six organs named.

steps.label: Internal morphology
lines: b) Internal morphology is the study of the
steps.why: The second branch looks inside the organs, and it subdivides — saying 'it has two branches' sets up histology and anatomy for the final mark.
common_mistakes: Ending here without the two sub-branches — the question asks for the salient features of each branch.
Calling internal morphology 'anatomy' directly — in this syllabus, anatomy is one of its two branches.
steps.memory_tip: External is one level; internal opens into two more — histology and anatomy.
steps.margin_note: Two lines; the sub-branches follow in the next step.

steps.label: Histology and anatomy
lines: i) Histology is the study of the different
tissues present in the plant body.
ii) Anatomy deals with the gross internal
details of plant organs such as root, stem
steps.why: The two sub-branches split by depth of view: histology reads tissues, anatomy reads the gross (whole-organ) internal plan — the syllabus framing the book prints.
common_mistakes: Swapping the two definitions — tissues go with histology; gross organ interiors go with anatomy.
Writing cytology here — cell study is a different branch and not part of this answer.
steps.memory_tip: Histo- means tissue, so histology is tissues; the other one, anatomy, takes the whole organ.
steps.margin_note: Both sub-branches defined, then the boxed summary line.

insider_note: Keep the outline lettering visible — a), b), i), ii) mirrors how the four marks are counted.
